Both flow readers describe a general-to-particular order (framing, thesis, roadmap, then table, connections, Veldmark, ending) with the chapters in a causal 'each acts on the one before' chain, which agrees with large_to_small plus prerequisite_order; neither marks any section unclear and neither proposes a reordering. Points both readers raised but judged not material for this audience: 'bumps' (A1, B2), Yardstick as the monolith (A2, B2), Casavista, Keybridge and Hearthly (A3, B3, B6) and the investor (B6) are all in audience.already_knows (Part VI's paid bumps; Veldmark in outline from meet-veldmark, which introduces the private-equity investor); the chapter-order-versus-date friction (A5, B5) is one both readers call a pause rather than a lost thread, and the draft states 'They are listed in chapter order, not by date' as the spec requires.

Reader A (A4) could not tell what the AI chapter takes from the migration, and How this part connects then ties AI to the ML platform and Part II's schemas, not to the migration, so the claimed chain does not visibly hold at this step. Naming what AI builds on (the spec's how_why: the gateway, model registry and services moved out of the monolith) would close it. Reported by reader A only.

results.finding: Reader B (B4) had to read the consolidation bullet twice to separate its three decisions and two parenthetical glosses. Reader A (A3) also re-read this line, but for a different reason: whether Keybridge belongs to the Casavista deal, which the audience knows from meet-veldmark; so this density point is not counted as corroborated. Splitting the decisions within the bullet would ease it.

Terms the cold readers stopped at ('bumps', Yardstick, Casavista, Keybridge, Hearthly, the investor) are in audience.already_knows. Of the does_not_know terms, 'federated under group controls' is glossed '(sharing finance and security only)' (B4 understood it from the gloss), the synergy ledger appears only as a decision 'in place of spreadsheets', the advice process, seams, gates and stressors are glossed in KEY POINTS as the spec states, and fitness functions are named as what the chapter builds. 'Integration option' and 'consolidation sequence' in the failure-pattern callout are used as plain phrases whose sense is clear in context (the intro reader paraphrased them correctly) and no reader reported them. Each paragraph opens from something already introduced.
The introduction opens on a direct statement continuing Part VII and states a disputable claim; it is not a placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.
The conclusion synthesizes, states the part's test and hands off; it does not open with 'in conclusion', add a new idea, carry body evidence or end on a restated thesis alone.
'Together, the chapters turn the diagram into owned, gated, measured changes' states what no single section states, and the so-what is the four-question test the reader can now apply to any change.
'turn the diagram into owned, gated, measured changes' returns to p01's 'whether that system ever exists outside a diagram', as callback.to names.

The intro-only reader named the five chapters in order (consolidation, organization, migration/modernization, AI across the listing lifecycle, long-term evolution over ten years) matching the expected subjects, predicted Veldmark and the earlier designs as evidence, and a declarative, prescriptive tone; the roadmap promises (table, then earlier designs, then Veldmark) were also predicted.
The reader named organizing-marketplace-engineering, ai-in-listing-systems and long-term-evolution for the three situations, as expected, and found each in the 'Read it when…' column.

The reader gave every expected dependency (tenancy model and release rings; context map; event contract and search platform as seams; ML platform and Part II taxonomy and schemas) and that Part IX tests the argument against publicly documented marketplace groups.
